questions.question: What is the difference between widening and narrowing type conversion in Java?
questions.title: Widening vs Narrowing Type Conversion in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Widening** is implicit — smaller type to larger type (`int → long → double`), done automatically with no data loss. **Narrowing** is explicit — larger type to smaller type (`double → int`), requires a cast, and may lose data through truncation or overflow.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java's type system and automatic vs manual conversions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that narrowing truncates (doesn't round) — (int) 3.9 gives 3, not 4
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the widening order byte → short → int → long → float → double, and explain why narrowing can lose data

sections.title: Going Up a Type Is Free; Coming Back Down Needs Your Signature
sections.content:
**Type conversion** in Java means changing a value from one data type into another — like turning a whole-number `int` into a decimal `double`, or squeezing a `double` back down into an `int`.

Java is strict about types. Every value has a fixed type: an `int` box can only hold whole numbers, a `double` box can hold decimals. But you often have a value of one type in a spot where another type is needed, so Java has to convert it. There are two directions this can go, and the direction decides everything. Going from a smaller type to a larger one is **widening**. Going from a larger type to a smaller one is **narrowing**.

Think of the types as a set of nesting cups, smallest to largest: `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`. Pouring water from a small cup into a big cup is always safe — the big cup has room to spare. Java does this for you automatically, with no extra syntax and no risk. That is **widening**. Pouring a big cup into a small cup is different: some water spills. Java refuses to do that silently, so it makes you write a **cast** — a small piece of syntax like `(int)` placed in front of the value — which is your way of saying "I know data might be lost, and I accept it." That is **narrowing**.

The **order worth memorizing** is `byte → short → int → long → float → double`. Every step to the right is a widening and happens automatically. Every step back to the left is a narrowing and needs a cast. So `int → long` is widening (no cast), while `double → int` is narrowing (you must write `(int)`). Widening carries no risk because the bigger type has more bits and can represent every value the smaller one holds — a `long` can store any `int` exactly.

Narrowing is where the surprises live, and it loses data in two different ways. The first is **truncation**: cast `9.99` to an `int` and the `.99` is simply dropped, so you get `9` — chopped, not rounded. The second is **overflow**: cast `300` into a `byte`, which only goes up to `127`, and the value wraps around silently to `44`, with no exception and no warning — just a wrong number. The point interviewers want to hear is that the **cast only silences the compiler**; it does not protect your value, so you should narrow only when you already know the number fits.

sections.title: The Type Hierarchy: Widening Goes Up Freely, Narrowing Goes Down With a Cast
sections.content:
Every arrow pointing upward in this diagram is a widening conversion — Java does it automatically. Every arrow pointing downward is a narrowing — you must write an explicit cast. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["byte
1 byte"] B["short
2 bytes"] C["int
4 bytes"] D["long
8 bytes"] E["float
4 bytes"] F["double
8 bytes"] A -->|"widening: automatic"| B B -->|"widening: automatic"| C C -->|"widening: automatic"| D D -->|"widening: automatic"| E E -->|"widening: automatic"| F F -.->|"narrowing: (int) cast needed"| C D -.->|"narrowing: (int) cast needed"| C C -.->|"narrowing: (byte) cast needed"| A ``` The solid arrows go up — those are safe and silent. The dashed arrows go down — those require your explicit cast. When you write `(int) someDouble`, you are taking one of those dashed arrows downward and telling Java you accept the consequences.

sections.title: Widening vs Narrowing Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Widening | Narrowing |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | Smaller to larger type | Larger to smaller type |
| Syntax | Implicit, automatic | Explicit cast required |
| Data loss | None — always safe | Possible truncation/overflow |
| Example | `int` to `long` | `double` to `int` |
| When | Assignment, method calls | Only with an explicit cast |

sections.title: The Line That Looks Harmless but Won't Compile
sections.content:
The most common first encounter with narrowing is an accident. You compute something as a `double`, then try to store it in an `int` without thinking about the gap between the two types.

```java
double d = 9.99;
int i = d; // COMPILE ERROR: narrowing requires an explicit cast
```

Java stops you here on purpose. It will not silently drop the `.99` for you — it makes you write the cast so the data loss is your decision, not a hidden side effect.

sections.title: Widening Just Works; Narrowing Asks You to Take Responsibility
sections.content:
Once you fix the line, the contrast becomes obvious. Widening assignments need nothing. Narrowing assignments need a cast in front, and that cast is your acknowledgement that something might be lost.

```java
long l = 100;        // widening: int -> long, implicit and safe
double big = l;      // widening: long -> double, implicit
int i = (int) 9.99;  // narrowing: explicit cast, truncates to 9
byte b = (byte) 300; // narrowing overflow: wraps to 44 (no exception)
```

Look closely at the last line — the cast compiles, runs, and gives you `44` with no warning at all. The cast silences the compiler; it does not protect the value. That is exactly why you only narrow when you have checked the value fits.

sections.title: When Each Conversion Happens
sections.content:
Use **widening** when storing a smaller value in a larger container — common when a method accepts `long` but you pass an `int`; Java handles it automatically.

Use **narrowing** when you intentionally extract a whole-number part (`double` to `int`) or read values you know fit in a smaller type. Always verify the value is within the target range before narrowing — narrowing appears often when processing input or interfacing with APIs that return larger types than needed.

sections.title: The Traps That Turn a Cast Into a Silent Bug
sections.content:
- **Expecting narrowing to round** — `(int) 7.8` gives `7`, not `8`; Java chops toward zero, so you silently lose `0.8` of value with no error.
- **Forgetting overflow wraps silently** — `(byte) 300` gives `44` because `byte` maxes at 127; there is no exception, just a wrong number that surfaces far away from the cast.
- **Trusting `long → float` to be lossless** — it is a widening so the compiler stays quiet, but `float` has only ~7 significant digits, so a large `long` loses precision even though no cast is required.
- **Assuming a cast makes the value safe** — the cast only silences the compiler; if the value does not fit the target range, the cast happily produces garbage.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Widening order** — `byte → short → int → long → float → double`, each step implicit.
- **Narrowing needs a cast** — `(targetType) value`, enforced by the compiler.
- **Truncation, not rounding** — `(int) 9.99` is `9`.
- **Overflow** — narrowing can wrap silently (no exception).
- **char widens to int** — 16-bit unsigned to 32-bit signed.
- **Constant exception** — `byte b = 10 + 20` compiles (30 fits).

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The way I think about it is **direction plus safety**. When you go from a smaller type to a larger one — `int` to `long`, or `long` to `double` — that's **widening**, and Java does it for you automatically with no cast, because the bigger type can hold every value the smaller one could. Nothing is at risk, so Java stays out of your way.

Going the other direction — `double` to `int`, or `int` to `byte` — is **narrowing**, and Java refuses to do it silently. You have to write the cast yourself, putting `(int)` in front of the value. That cast is basically your signature saying you accept that data might be lost. And it really can be lost two ways. Casting `9.99` to an `int` gives you `9`, not `10`, because it **truncates toward zero** rather than rounding — that's the one freshers get wrong most often. And casting `300` to a `byte` gives you `44`, because `byte` only goes to `127` and the value wraps with no exception at all.

The order worth memorizing is `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double` — every step rightward is free, every step back needs a cast. The key insight I'd leave them with: **the cast silences the compiler, it doesn't protect your value**. So I only narrow when I've already checked the number actually fits.

questions.question: How do you convert a String to an int and an int to a String in Java?
questions.title: String to int and int to String Conversion in Java
questions.direct_answer: **String to int**: use `Integer.parseInt(str)` for a primitive `int`, or `Integer.valueOf(str)` for an `Integer` object. **Int to String**: use `String.valueOf(num)`, `Integer.toString(num)`, or `"" + num`. `parseInt` throws **`NumberFormatException`** if the string isn't a valid number.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Java knowledge — type conversion is done in almost every real application
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Integer.parseInt on a non-numeric string without try-catch, or casting a String to int directly (which doesn't work)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish parseInt (returns primitive) vs valueOf (returns Integer object), and mention NumberFormatException handling

sections.title: Why You Can't Cast "42" to a Number — You Have to Parse It
sections.content:
**Converting a `String` to an `int`** means taking text like `"42"` and turning it into the actual number `42` you can do math with — and going the other way turns a number back into text. This comes up constantly, so Java gives you dedicated tools for it. The first surprise is what does *not* work: you might try `(int) "42"`, expecting it to behave like a normal cast, and the compiler rejects it instantly. That rejection confuses people, because casting works fine between `double` and `int`. So why not here?

Because a `String` and an `int` are **not related types** in Java. You cannot cast one to the other. Casting is a type-hierarchy operation — it only works between types that have an inheritance relationship. `String` is a class. `int` is a primitive. They have nothing in common in Java's type system, so there is no "hierarchy step" to take between them.

So when you want to go from text to number, you are not casting. You are **parsing**. Parsing means reading the characters one by one — the `'4'` and the `'2'` — and computing the numeric value `42`. That is a completely different operation, and Java gives you a dedicated tool for it: **`Integer.parseInt()`**.

When you call `Integer.parseInt("42")`, Java reads the string, confirms each character is a valid digit, and returns the primitive `int` value `42`. If the string is `"12abc"` or empty, it cannot compute a number, so it throws a **`NumberFormatException`** — an unchecked exception you should catch whenever the input comes from a user or external source.

There is a **close cousin**: **`Integer.valueOf("42")`**. The difference is small but matters. `parseInt` returns a primitive `int`. `valueOf` returns an `Integer` object — the wrapper class. In most code you will not care because Java auto-unboxes `Integer` to `int`. But `valueOf` also caches `Integer` objects for the range `-128` to `127`, which can save memory when you convert the same small numbers repeatedly. For getting an `int` value, `parseInt` is the default choice.

Going the other direction — from `int` to `String` — is **easier**, with three clean options:

- **`String.valueOf(42)`** — pass the number, get the string `"42"` back; the cleanest, most readable choice.
- **`Integer.toString(42)`** — does exactly the same thing.
- `"" + 42` — concatenating with an empty string; this works but is considered less clear because it relies on Java's string concatenation operator, not an explicit conversion call.

Prefer `String.valueOf` in production code because the intent is obvious.

Converting between `String` and `int` comes up **constantly** in Java — reading form input, parsing config files, building URL parameters, formatting log messages. Getting comfortable with `parseInt` and `String.valueOf` is one of the most practical skills for a working Java developer.

sections.title: String ↔ int Conversion: Two Different Tools for Two Different Directions
sections.content:
The diagram below shows the two conversion paths. Notice that casting is crossed out — it does not work here. Each direction has its own dedicated tool. ```mermaid flowchart LR STR["\"42\"
(String)"] NUM["42
(int)"] OBJ["Integer
(object)"] STR -->|"Integer.parseInt()
→ primitive int"| NUM STR -->|"Integer.valueOf()
→ Integer object"| OBJ OBJ -->|"auto-unboxing"| NUM NUM -->|"String.valueOf()
or Integer.toString()"| STR CAST["(int) str
COMPILE ERROR"] style CAST fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,color:#991b1b ``` ParseInt is your go-to for String → int. String.valueOf is your go-to for int → String. The red box is the thing freshers try that does not compile.

sections.title: String / int Conversion at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|String to int|~parseInt(str)|returns a primitive int|valueOf returns Integer|the common case
blue|int to String|~String.valueOf(n)|Integer.toString(n)|"" + n (less clear)|preferred: valueOf
emerald|Failure|~NumberFormatException|on "12abc"|wrap untrusted input|trim it first

sections.title: The Line Everyone Tries First That Refuses to Compile
sections.content:
The instinct is to treat text-to-number like any other conversion and slap a cast in front of it. Java rejects it before the program ever runs.

```java
String text = "42";
int n = (int) text; // COMPILE ERROR: cannot cast String to int
```

This is not a runtime surprise you can catch — it is a hard compile error, because `String` and `int` share no inheritance relationship for the cast to walk.

sections.title: The Four Calls That Cover Almost Every Real Conversion
When to Use Each Method
sections.content:
Use **`Integer.parseInt()`** when you need a primitive `int` — console input, request parameters, CSV data; it avoids object overhead.

Use **`Integer.valueOf()`** when you need an `Integer` object — storing in `List<Integer>`, leveraging the `-128..127` cache.

For int to String, prefer **`String.valueOf()`** for clarity (null-safe). Use **`Integer.toString()`** when you need a radix. Always wrap `parseInt` in try-catch when parsing untrusted input.

sections.title: Where String-to-int Conversions Blow Up in Production
sections.content:
- **Calling `parseInt` on untrusted input without a try-catch** — `Integer.parseInt("abc")` throws `NumberFormatException`, an unchecked exception that will crash the request if you assumed the string was clean.
- **Reaching for a cast instead of parsing** — `(int) "42"` does not compile because `String` and `int` are unrelated types; casting is for type hierarchies, not for interpreting text.
- **Forgetting embedded whitespace still fails** — `"  42  "` parses fine after trimming, but `"4 2"` with a space in the middle throws; always `trim()` external input and validate it can never contain inner spaces.
- **Using `valueOf` in a hot loop over thousands of values** — it autoboxes into an `Integer` object every time outside the `-128..127` cache, adding allocation pressure where `parseInt` would have stayed on the stack.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **parseInt** — returns a primitive `int`.
- **valueOf** — returns an `Integer` (cached for `-128..127`).
- **NumberFormatException** — unchecked; handle for untrusted input.
- **String.valueOf** — preferred for int to String.
- **Radix** — `parseInt`/`toString` accept bases 2–36.
- **No direct cast** — `(int) "42"` won't compile.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The first thing I'd point out is that **you don't cast here — you parse**. People expect to write open-paren int close-paren on the string, but a `String` and an `int` aren't related types, so that won't even compile. Casting walks a type hierarchy; turning text into a number is a different job entirely.

So to go from `String` to `int`, I use **`Integer.parseInt`** — pass the string, get a primitive `int` back. If I actually need the wrapper object, say for a `List` of `Integer`, I'd use `Integer.valueOf` instead, which returns an `Integer` and caches the small values from minus 128 to 127. The thing I never skip: `parseInt` throws a **`NumberFormatException`** the moment the string isn't a clean number — letters, an embedded space, anything. So any time the input comes from a user, a request, or a file, I **wrap it in a `try-catch` and trim it first**. That's the line between code that works in a demo and code that survives real input.

Going back the other way is easier — `String.valueOf` of the number is my default because the intent is obvious; `Integer.toString` does the same and also takes a radix if I need hex. I'd close on that distinction: **`parseInt` for the primitive, `valueOf` for the object**, and always guard the parse on anything you didn't generate yourself.

questions.question: What happens when you cast a double 9.99 to an int in Java — does it round or truncate?
questions.title: Truncation vs Rounding in Java double to int Cast
questions.direct_answer: Java **truncates** (does not round) when casting a `double` to `int`. `(int) 9.99` gives `9`, and `(int) -3.7` gives `-3` (not `-4`) — the fractional part is discarded toward zero. To round properly, use `Math.round()` first.

interviewer_intent.testing: A classic output-prediction gotcha — truncation vs rounding surprises many freshers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting (int) 9.9 to give 10 — it gives 9; truncation always goes toward zero
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Math.round() for nearest-integer rounding, and Math.ceil()/Math.floor() for ceiling/floor

sections.title: The Cast Operator Is a Chopper, Not a Rounder
sections.content:
When you cast a decimal number like `9.99` to an `int`, Java **throws away everything after the decimal point** and keeps only the whole-number part — so you get `9`, not `10`. This shows up in output-prediction questions constantly because the answer feels wrong. You see `(int) 9.99` and your brain says "that's basically 10." Java disagrees, and the reason is worth getting straight once and for all.

When you cast a `double` to an `int` in Java, one thing happens: the fractional part is thrown away. Not rounded. Not averaged. Just gone. This is called **truncation** — cutting off everything after the decimal point.

So `(int) 9.99` gives you `9`. Not `10`. Even though `9.99` is much closer to `10` than to `9`, **the cast does not care about closeness**. It simply takes the whole-number part and discards the rest.

The same rule applies to negative numbers, but this is where freshers often get surprised. `(int) -3.7` gives `-3`, not `-4`. Why? Because truncation always moves **toward zero**. Negative `3.7` is between `-4` and `-3` on the number line. Moving toward zero means going to `-3`. The fraction `.7` is dropped.

This is different from `Math.floor(-3.7)`, which gives `-4`. **Floor always rounds down** — toward negative infinity. Truncation goes toward zero. For positive numbers, truncation and floor give the same result. For negative numbers, they differ. That distinction is a classic interview trick.

Why does Java truncate instead of round? **Speed.** Casting a `double` to an `int` maps to a single CPU instruction. Rounding requires comparison logic: is the fraction above or below 0.5? The cast operator is meant to be fast and mechanical, not smart.

If you want proper rounding, you must be explicit about it. Java gives you three tools:

- **`Math.round()`** — rounds to the nearest integer. `Math.round(9.99)` gives `10`. Returns a `long`, so cast it: `(int) Math.round(9.99)`.
- **`Math.ceil()`** — always rounds up toward positive infinity. `Math.ceil(9.1)` is `10.0`.
- **`Math.floor()`** — always rounds down toward negative infinity. `Math.floor(9.9)` is `9.0`.

**A practical example**: if you are writing code to calculate how many pages a list needs — say 101 results at 10 per page — you need `Math.ceil(101.0 / 10)` which gives `11`. If you used a cast, you would get `10` and silently lose one page.

**For money and financial calculations, never rely on any of these.** Use `BigDecimal` with an explicit `RoundingMode` to control exactly how rounding works.

The one-sentence rule to remember: **the cast operator truncates toward zero; use `Math.round` if you want nearest-integer behavior.**

sections.content:
The diagram traces exactly what the JVM does when it executes `(int) 9.99`. There is no intelligence here — just mechanical removal of the decimal part. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["9.99
(double)"] B["Drop the
fractional part
(.99 is gone)"] C["9
(int)"] A -->|"(int) cast"| B B -->|"result"| C D["9.99 is closer to 10
but we still get 9"] C -.->|"not rounded"| D style D fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,color:#92400e ``` And here is the negative-number case that trips people up: ```mermaid flowchart LR X["-3.7
(double)"] Y["Truncate toward zero
(-.7 is gone)"] Z["-3
(int)"] X -->|"(int) cast"| Y Y -->|"result"| Z W["Math.floor(-3.7)
would give -4"] Z -.->|"differs from floor"| W style W fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6,color:#1e3a8a ``` For positive numbers, truncation and floor give the same answer. For negative numbers they differ. That is the gotcha.

sections.title: Cast vs Round at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Cast double to int|~Truncates|(int) 9.99 is 9|drops the fraction|fast, single instruction
blue|Toward zero|~Not floor|(int) -3.7 is -3|not -4|differs from Math.floor
emerald|Round properly|~Math.round()|returns a long|cast to int|nearest integer
rose|Ceil and floor|~Math.ceil rounds up|Math.floor rounds down|capacity/pagination|money: use BigDecimal

sections.title: Every Rounding Behavior Side by Side
sections.content:
Seeing all four behaviors in one place makes the differences click — the same two numbers run through a plain cast, `Math.round`, `Math.ceil`, and `Math.floor` so you can compare the outputs directly.

```java
public class DoubleTruncationDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println((int) 9.99);        // 9   — truncates
        System.out.println((int) -3.7);        // -3  — toward zero, not -4

        System.out.println((int) Math.round(9.99)); // 10 — nearest
        System.out.println((int) Math.round(-3.7)); // -4 — nearest

        System.out.println((int) Math.ceil(9.1));   // 10 — round up
        System.out.println((int) Math.floor(9.9));  // 9  — round down
    }
}
```

The pair to stare at is `(int) -3.7` giving `-3` while `Math.floor(-3.7)` gives `-4` — that single divergence between truncation and floor on negatives is the exact trap interviewers set.

sections.title: The Bug: Trusting the Cast to Do Your Rounding
sections.content:
This is the line that quietly produces wrong totals. The variable is even named `rounded`, which is exactly what the developer assumed would happen.

```java
double price = 9.99;
int rounded = (int) price; // 9 — NOT 10; the cast truncates
```

The code compiles, runs, and ships — it just gives the wrong number. There is no error to catch, which is why this kind of bug survives all the way to production reports that are off by a cent or a unit.

sections.title: The Fix: Say "Round" When You Mean Round
sections.content:
If you want nearest-integer behavior, ask for it explicitly. `Math.round` does the comparison the cast refuses to do.

```java
double price = 9.99;
int rounded = (int) Math.round(price); // 10 — nearest integer
```

One detail trips people here: `Math.round` returns a `long`, so you still cast it to `int`. Reach for `Math.ceil` when you must always round up — like pages or boxes — and `Math.floor` when you must always round down.

sections.title: When Truncation Matters
sections.content:
Use direct casting **`(int) value`** when you want to **discard the fraction** — extracting whole units or intentionally rounding down.

Use **`Math.round()`** for **nearest-integer** rounding (dollar amounts, percentages). Use **`Math.ceil()`** to **round up** (boxes needed, pagination — 101 results at 10/page need 11 pages). Use **`Math.floor()`** to **round down** (clearer than casting for negatives). For money, never rely on casting alone — use explicit rounding or `BigDecimal`.

sections.title: The Off-by-One Bugs Truncation Loves to Cause
sections.content:
- **Expecting the cast to round** — `(int) 7.8` gives `7`, not `8`; the missing `0.8` becomes a silent rounding-down error with no warning.
- **Assuming negatives behave like floor** — `(int) -3.7` gives `-3` because truncation goes toward zero, while `Math.floor(-3.7)` gives `-4`; mixing them up flips your result by one.
- **Truncating in a pagination or capacity calc** — `(int)(101.0 / 10)` gives `10` pages and silently drops the last record; you need `Math.ceil` to get `11`.
- **Casting money instead of using `BigDecimal`** — a plain cast on a currency `double` loses the cents entirely, so financial totals must round explicitly or use `BigDecimal` with a `RoundingMode`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Truncation, not rounding** — the fraction is discarded.
- **Toward zero** — `(int) 9.9` is `9`; `(int) -3.7` is `-3`.
- **Math.round** — nearest integer (returns `long`).
- **Math.ceil** — rounds up; **Math.floor** — rounds down.
- **Negatives differ** — truncation ≠ floor for negatives.
- **Money** — use explicit rounding or `BigDecimal`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
**It truncates — it doesn't round.** So casting `9.99` to an `int` gives you `9`, not `10`. The cast just chops off everything after the decimal point; it never looks at whether you're closer to `9` or `10`. People expect rounding because that's what feels mathematically right, but the cast is deliberately mechanical and fast — it's a single CPU instruction, not a decision.

The part I'd make sure to mention is negatives, because that's where it gets subtle. **Truncation always moves toward zero**, so open-paren int close-paren on negative 3.7 gives negative 3, not negative 4. That's different from `Math.floor`, which would give negative 4 because floor goes toward negative infinity. For positives they happen to agree, but on negatives they split — and that's the exact gotcha interviewers love.

If I actually want rounding, I say so: **`Math.round` for nearest** — remembering it returns a `long` so I cast that to `int` — `Math.ceil` when I always need to round up, and `Math.floor` when I always need to round down. Ceil is the one for capacity math, like 101 results at 10 per page needing 11 pages, not 10. And **for anything touching money I wouldn't lean on a cast at all**; I'd round explicitly or use `BigDecimal`, because a silent truncation there is a bug that ships.
